title: Inpainting physics: self-supervised learning for context-driven fluid simulation
claim: Learn a self-supervised prior over tokenised fields, then impose constraints only at inference by fixing known context and inpainting the rest.
layout: 3 boxed panels, left-to-right; colored sub-panels for two training variants
description: A wide three-panel figure read left to right, each panel in a rounded box with a numbered title. Panel 1, 'Neighbourhood tokeniser', shows a 3D aneurysm vessel with velocity arrows colored by a blue-to-yellow velocity colorbar. A downward arrow leads to the same shape built from colored spheres labelled 'Local latent tokens'. Panel 2, 'Self-supervised training', has two tinted sub-panels. The blue one, 'Latent flow matching', shows grey noisy spheres denoised step by step into a colored shape. The orange one, 'Latent masked autoencoder', shows a red masked sphere shape reconstructed into a colored one. Panel 3, 'Context-driven inpainting', has two grey sub-boxes. 'Explicit boundary conditions' shows fixed inflow/outflow regions inpainted into a full flow field. 'Local geometry edit' shows a deformed aneurysm bulge. The eye goes first to the colorful vessel renders and the spheres.
caption: Inpainting physics. (1) We tokenise raw velocity fields into local ball-shaped latent representations. (2) We train a self-supervised model on these tokenised velocity fields using latent flow matching or a masked autoencoder. (3) At inference, known regions (e.g., inflow and outflow, measurements, or unchanged parts of a previous simulation) are fixed as context and the rest is inpainted, enabling generalisation to unseen geometries and flow conditions, preserving local flow structure.
abstract: Neural surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are typically trained as forward operators that map explicit problem specifications, such as geometry and boundary conditions, to solution fields. This ties the model to the conditioning variables seen during training and limits reuse under boundary-condition shifts or local geometry changes. We propose to reformulate steady CFD inference as an inpainting problem: instead of training on explicit boundary conditions, we learn a self-supervised prior over velocity fields and impose boundary constraints only during inference by fixing known regions such as inlet, outlet or unchanged regions from previous simulations. To scale this idea to large 3D meshes, we introduce a local neighbourhood tokeniser that represents high-resolution velocity fields as compact spatial latent tokens and train latent flow-matching and masked-autoencoder models on these tokens. On simulations of intracranial aneurysm flow, our method reconstructs full velocity fields from sparse boundary context, outperforms supervised neural surrogates under boundary-condition and dataset shift and enables local geometry editing by reusing unchanged simulation context. These results suggest that viewing CFD inference as context-conditioned inpainting can turn neural surrogates from task-specific predictors into reusable flow priors. Code and demo are available at https://inpainting-physics.com.
